questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: A concave mirror with a radius of curvature of $40 \text{ cm}$ is positioned in front of an illuminated point source at a distance of $30 \text{ cm}$ from it. Determine the location of the image.
options: $60 \text{ cm}$ from the mirror on the side of the object
$60 \text{ cm}$ from the mirror on the opposite side of the object
$120 \text{ cm}$ from the mirror on the opposite side of the object
$12 \text{ cm}$ from the mirror on the side of the object
questions.solution:
Given, radius of curvature of the concave mirror, $R = -40 \text{ cm}$

Focal length, $f = \dfrac{R}{2} = -20 \text{ cm}$

Object distance, $u = -30 \text{ cm}$

Using the mirror formula:

$\dfrac{1}{v} + \dfrac{1}{u} = \dfrac{1}{f}$

$\dfrac{1}{v} + \dfrac{1}{-30} = \dfrac{1}{-20}$

$\dfrac{1}{v} = \dfrac{1}{30} - \dfrac{1}{20}$

$\dfrac{1}{v} = \dfrac{2 - 3}{60} = -\dfrac{1}{60}$

$v = -60 \text{ cm}$

The negative sign indicates that the image is formed in front of the mirror, which is on the same side as the object. Therefore, the image is located $60 \text{ cm}$ from the mirror on the side of the object.

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: A $1 \text{ cm}$ object is placed perpendicular to the principal axis of a convex mirror of focal length $7.5 \text{ cm}$. Determine its distance from the mirror if the resulting image is $0.6 \text{ cm}$ in size.
questions.solution:
Given $h_{o} = 1 \text{ cm}$, $f = +7.5 \text{ cm}$, and $h_{i} = +0.6 \text{ cm}$ (virtual and erect image for a convex mirror).

Magnification $m = \dfrac{h_{i}}{h_{o}} = \dfrac{0.6}{1} = 0.6$

Using $m = -\dfrac{v}{u}$, we get $v = -0.6u$.

Applying the mirror formula:

$\dfrac{1}{v} + \dfrac{1}{u} = \dfrac{1}{f}$

$\dfrac{1}{-0.6u} + \dfrac{1}{u} = \dfrac{1}{7.5}$

$\dfrac{-1 + 0.6}{0.6u} = \dfrac{1}{7.5}$

$\dfrac{-0.4}{0.6u} = \dfrac{1}{7.5}$

$\dfrac{-2}{3u} = \dfrac{1}{7.5}$

$3u = -15 \Rightarrow u = -5 \text{ cm}$

The distance of the object from the mirror is $5 \text{ cm}$.

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: A candle flame $1.6 \text{ cm}$ high is imaged in a ball bearing of diameter $0.4 \text{ cm}$. If the ball bearing is $20 \text{ cm}$ away from the flame, determine the location and the height of the image.
options: $1.0 \text{ mm}$ outside the ball bearing, $0.08 \text{ mm}$
$2.0 \text{ mm}$ inside the ball bearing, $0.16 \text{ mm}$
$1.0 \text{ mm}$ inside the ball bearing, $0.08 \text{ mm}$
$0.1 \text{ mm}$ inside the ball bearing, $0.008 \text{ mm}$
questions.solution:
The ball bearing acts as a convex mirror.

Radius of curvature $R = \dfrac{0.4}{2} = 0.2 \text{ cm}$.

Focal length $f = \dfrac{R}{2} = +0.1 \text{ cm}$.

Object distance $u = -20 \text{ cm}$.

Using the mirror formula:

$\dfrac{1}{v} + \dfrac{1}{u} = \dfrac{1}{f}$

$\dfrac{1}{v} - \dfrac{1}{20} = \dfrac{1}{0.1} = 10$

$\dfrac{1}{v} = 10 + \dfrac{1}{20} = \dfrac{201}{20}$

$v = \dfrac{20}{201} \text{ cm} \approx 0.1 \text{ cm} = 1.0 \text{ mm}$

Since $v > 0$, the image is virtual and formed $1.0 \text{ mm}$ inside the ball bearing.

Magnification $m = -\dfrac{v}{u}$

$m = -\dfrac{20/201}{-20} = \dfrac{1}{201}$

Height of the image $h_i = m \times h_o$

$h_i = \dfrac{1}{201} \times 1.6 \text{ cm} \approx \dfrac{1.6}{200} \text{ cm} = 0.008 \text{ cm} = 0.08 \text{ mm}$

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: A concave mirror produces an image of a $20 \text{ cm}$ high object on a screen located $5.0 \text{ m}$ from the mirror. The height of the image is $50 \text{ cm}$. Determine the focal length of the mirror and the distance between the mirror and the object.
questions.solution:
Given that the image is formed on a screen, it is a real and inverted image.

Height of the object, $h_o = 20 \text{ cm} = 0.2 \text{ m}$

Height of the image, $h_i = -50 \text{ cm} = -0.5 \text{ m}$

Image distance, $v = -5.0 \text{ m}$

Magnification, $m = \dfrac{h_i}{h_o} = \dfrac{-0.5}{0.2} = -2.5$

Using the relation $m = -\dfrac{v}{u}$:

$-2.5 = -\dfrac{-5.0}{u} \Rightarrow u = -2.0 \text{ m}$

The distance between the mirror and the object is $2.0 \text{ m}$.

Using the mirror formula $\dfrac{1}{f} = \dfrac{1}{v} + \dfrac{1}{u}$:

$\dfrac{1}{f} = \dfrac{1}{-5.0} + \dfrac{1}{-2.0} = -0.2 - 0.5 = -0.7 \text{ m}^{-1}$

$f = -\dfrac{1}{0.7} \approx -1.43 \text{ m}$

The focal length of the mirror is $1.43 \text{ m}$.

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: A concave mirror possesses a focal length of $20 \text{ cm}$. Determine the position or positions of an object such that the image-size is double the object-size.
questions.solution:
Given the focal length of the concave mirror, $f = -20 \text{ cm}$.

The magnification produced by a mirror is given by $m = \dfrac{f}{f - u}$.

Since the image size is double the object size, the magnification can be either $m = -2$ (real image) or $m = +2$ (virtual image).

Case 1: For a real image, $m = -2$

$-2 = \dfrac{-20}{-20 - u}$

$40 + 2u = -20$

$2u = -60 \Rightarrow u = -30 \text{ cm}$

Case 2: For a virtual image, $m = +2$

$2 = \dfrac{-20}{-20 - u}$

$-40 - 2u = -20$

$-2u = 20 \Rightarrow u = -10 \text{ cm}$

The object can be placed at $10 \text{ cm}$ or $30 \text{ cm}$ from the mirror.

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: An object that is $3 \text{ cm}$ tall is positioned at a distance of $7.5 \text{ cm}$ from a convex mirror with a focal length of $6 \text{ cm}$. Determine the location, size, and nature of the image formed.
options: $\dfrac{10}{3} \text{ cm}$ in front of the mirror, $1.33 \text{ cm}$, real and inverted
$30 \text{ cm}$ in front of the mirror, $12 \text{ cm}$, real and inverted
$30 \text{ cm}$ behind the mirror, $12 \text{ cm}$, virtual and erect
$\dfrac{10}{3} \text{ cm}$ behind the mirror, $1.33 \text{ cm}$, virtual and erect
questions.solution:
Using the mirror formula, $\dfrac{1}{v} + \dfrac{1}{u} = \dfrac{1}{f}$

Given $u = -7.5 \text{ cm}$ and $f = +6 \text{ cm}$ for a convex mirror:

$\dfrac{1}{v} = \dfrac{1}{6} - \dfrac{1}{-7.5} = \dfrac{1}{6} + \dfrac{1}{7.5} = \dfrac{1}{6} + \dfrac{2}{15}$

$\dfrac{1}{v} = \dfrac{5 + 4}{30} = \dfrac{9}{30} = \dfrac{3}{10}$

$v = \dfrac{10}{3} \text{ cm}$

Since $v$ is positive, the image is formed $\dfrac{10}{3} \text{ cm}$ behind the mirror.

Magnification $m = -\dfrac{v}{u} = -\dfrac{\dfrac{10}{3}}{-7.5} = \dfrac{10}{3 \times 7.5} = \dfrac{10}{22.5} = \dfrac{4}{9}$

Height of the image $h_i = m \times h_o = \dfrac{4}{9} \times 3 \text{ cm} = \dfrac{4}{3} \text{ cm} \approx 1.33 \text{ cm}$

Since $m$ is positive, the image is virtual and erect.

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: As depicted in the figure, a U-shaped wire is situated in front of a concave mirror with a radius of curvature of $20\text{ cm}$. Calculate the total length of the image.
questions.solution:
For the concave mirror, the focal length is $f = -\dfrac{R}{2} = -\dfrac{20}{2} = -10\text{ cm}$.

The U-shaped wire consists of three segments: two vertical and one horizontal.

1. For the right vertical segment:
Object distance, $u_1 = -30\text{ cm}$.
Using the mirror formula, $\dfrac{1}{v_1} + \dfrac{1}{u_1} = \dfrac{1}{f}$
$\dfrac{1}{v_1} - \dfrac{1}{30} = -\dfrac{1}{10} \Rightarrow \dfrac{1}{v_1} = \dfrac{1}{30} - \dfrac{1}{10} = -\dfrac{2}{30}$
$v_1 = -15\text{ cm}$
Magnification, $m_1 = -\dfrac{v_1}{u_1} = -\dfrac{-15}{-30} = -\dfrac{1}{2}$
Length of its image, $L_1 = |m_1| \times h_o = \dfrac{1}{2} \times 10 = 5\text{ cm}$.

2. For the left vertical segment:
Object distance, $u_2 = -(30 + 10) = -40\text{ cm}$.
$\dfrac{1}{v_2} - \dfrac{1}{40} = -\dfrac{1}{10} \Rightarrow \dfrac{1}{v_2} = \dfrac{1}{40} - \dfrac{1}{10} = -\dfrac{3}{40}$
$v_2 = -\dfrac{40}{3}\text{ cm}$
Magnification, $m_2 = -\dfrac{v_2}{u_2} = -\dfrac{-40/3}{-40} = -\dfrac{1}{3}$
Length of its image, $L_2 = |m_2| \times h_o = \dfrac{1}{3} \times 10 = \dfrac{10}{3}\text{ cm}$.

3. For the horizontal segment:
This segment lies along the principal axis from $u_1 = -30\text{ cm}$ to $u_2 = -40\text{ cm}$.
Its image lies along the principal axis from $v_1 = -15\text{ cm}$ to $v_2 = -\dfrac{40}{3}\text{ cm}$.
Length of its image, $L_3 = |v_1 - v_2| = \left|-15 - \left(-\dfrac{40}{3}\right)\right| = \left|-15 + \dfrac{40}{3}\right| = \dfrac{5}{3}\text{ cm}$.

Total length of the image is the sum of the lengths of these three segments:
$L = L_1 + L_2 + L_3 = 5 + \dfrac{10}{3} + \dfrac{5}{3} = 5 + \dfrac{15}{3} = 5 + 5 = 10\text{ cm}$.

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: Determine the diameter of the image of the moon produced by a spherical concave mirror having a focal length of $7.6 \text{ m}$. The moon's diameter is $3450 \text{ km}$ and the distance between the earth and the moon is $3.8 \times 10^5 \text{ km}$.
questions.solution:
Given, focal length of the mirror, $f = 7.6 \text{ m}$

Diameter of the moon, $D_o = 3450 \text{ km} = 3.45 \times 10^6 \text{ m}$

Distance of the moon from the mirror, $u = 3.8 \times 10^5 \text{ km} = 3.8 \times 10^8 \text{ m}$

Since the moon is at a very large distance, its image is formed at the focus of the concave mirror.

Image distance, $v \approx f = 7.6 \text{ m}$

The angle subtended by the object at the pole of the mirror is equal to the angle subtended by the image at the pole.

$\theta = \dfrac{D_o}{u} = \dfrac{D_i}{v}$

Substituting the values:

$\dfrac{3.45 \times 10^6}{3.8 \times 10^8} = \dfrac{D_i}{7.6}$

$D_i = 7.6 \times \dfrac{3.45 \times 10^6}{3.8 \times 10^8}$

$D_i = 2 \times 3.45 \times 10^{-2} \text{ m}$

$D_i = 6.9 \times 10^{-2} \text{ m}$

$D_i = 6.9 \text{ cm}$

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: A person uses a concave mirror for shaving. He places his face at a distance of $25 \text{ cm}$ from the mirror and obtains an image that is $1.4$ times enlarged. Determine the focal length of the mirror.
questions.solution:
For a shaving mirror, the image formed is virtual, erect, and enlarged. Therefore, the magnification is positive.

Given $u = -25 \text{ cm}$ and $m = +1.4$.

Using the relation between magnification, focal length, and object distance:

$m = \dfrac{f}{f - u}$

Substituting the values:

$1.4 = \dfrac{f}{f - (-25)}$

$1.4(f + 25) = f$

$1.4f + 35 = f$

$0.4f = -35$

$f = -\dfrac{35}{0.4} = -87.5 \text{ cm}$

The focal length of the concave mirror is $87.5 \text{ cm}$.

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: A particle travels in a circle of radius $2.0 \text{ cm}$. A concave mirror having a focal length of $20 \text{ cm}$ is positioned so that its principal axis passes through the centre of the circle and is perpendicular to its plane. The distance from the pole of the mirror to the centre of the circle is $30 \text{ cm}$. Determine the radius of the circle traced by the image.
questions.solution:
Using the mirror formula, $\dfrac{1}{v} + \dfrac{1}{u} = \dfrac{1}{f}$

Given $u = -30 \text{ cm}$ and $f = -20 \text{ cm}$

$\dfrac{1}{v} = \dfrac{1}{-20} - \dfrac{1}{-30} = \dfrac{-3 + 2}{60} = -\dfrac{1}{60}$

$v = -60 \text{ cm}$

The transverse magnification is given by $m = -\dfrac{v}{u}$

$m = -\dfrac{-60}{-30} = -2$

The radius of the circle traced by the image is the transverse height of the image.

$R_{image} = |m| \times R_{object}$

$R_{image} = |-2| \times 2.0 \text{ cm} = 4.0 \text{ cm}$

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: As depicted in the figure, a concave mirror of radius $R$ is placed on a horizontal table. Water (refractive index $= \mu$) is poured into the mirror up to a height $h$. At what position should an object be placed such that its image forms on itself?
questions.solution:
For the final image to form on the object itself, the light rays must retrace their path after reflection from the concave mirror.

This happens when the rays strike the mirror normally, which means the refracted rays must appear to come from the center of curvature $C$ of the mirror.

The center of curvature $C$ is at a distance $R$ from the pole of the mirror. Since the water is filled up to a height $h$, the distance of $C$ above the water surface is $R - h$.

Let the object be placed at a height $x$ above the water surface. When viewed from the water (denser medium), the apparent height of the object due to refraction at the plane surface is given by:
Apparent height $= \mu x$

For the rays to appear to come from $C$, this apparent height must be equal to the distance of $C$ from the water surface:
$\mu x = R - h$

$x = \dfrac{R - h}{\mu}$

Thus, the object should be placed at a distance of $\dfrac{R - h}{\mu}$ above the water surface.

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: As shown in the figure, a point source $S$ is positioned midway between two converging mirrors having equal focal length $f$. Determine the values of $d$ for which only a single image is formed.
questions.solution:
For a single image to be formed, the images produced by both mirrors must coincide.

Let the distance between the mirrors be $d$. The point source $S$ is placed midway, so the object distance for each mirror is $u = -\dfrac{d}{2}$.

Using the mirror formula for one of the concave mirrors (with focal length $F = -f$):
$\dfrac{1}{v} + \dfrac{1}{u} = \dfrac{1}{F}$
$\dfrac{1}{v} - \dfrac{2}{d} = -\dfrac{1}{f}$
$\dfrac{1}{v} = \dfrac{2}{d} - \dfrac{1}{f} = \dfrac{2f - d}{df}$
$v = -\dfrac{df}{d - 2f}$

The negative sign indicates the image is formed at a distance $\dfrac{df}{d - 2f}$ in front of the mirror. By symmetry, the second mirror forms its image at the same distance.

Case 1: The images coincide at a finite distance.
For the two images to coincide, they must meet at the same point in space. By symmetry, they must meet at the midpoint. Thus, the distance of each image from its respective mirror must be $\dfrac{d}{2}$.
$\dfrac{df}{d - 2f} = \dfrac{d}{2}$
$\dfrac{2f}{d - 2f} = 1 \Rightarrow 2f = d - 2f \Rightarrow d = 4f$
Here, the images coincide exactly at the position of the source $S$.

Case 2: The images coincide at infinity.
This occurs when the reflected rays are parallel, meaning the object is placed at the principal focus of both mirrors.
$\dfrac{d}{2} = f \Rightarrow d = 2f$

Thus, the values of $d$ for which only a single image is formed are $2f$ and $4f$.

Answer: $2f, 4f$

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: A converging mirror $M_1$, a point source $S$, and a diverging mirror $M_2$ are configured as shown in the figure. The source is located at a distance of $30 \text{ cm}$ from $M_1$. Each mirror has a focal length of $20 \text{ cm}$. Taking into account only the images produced by at most two reflections, it is observed that one image coincides with the source itself. Determine the distance separating the two mirrors.
questions.solution:
For the converging (concave) mirror $M_1$, the focal length is $f_1 = -20 \text{ cm}$.
For the diverging (convex) mirror $M_2$, the focal length is $f_2 = +20 \text{ cm}$.
Let the distance between the two mirrors be $d$.

Consider the first reflection at $M_1$:
The object (source $S$) is at a distance of $30 \text{ cm}$ from $M_1$, so $u_1 = -30 \text{ cm}$.
Using the mirror formula for $M_1$:
$\dfrac{1}{v_1} + \dfrac{1}{u_1} = \dfrac{1}{f_1}$
$\dfrac{1}{v_1} - \dfrac{1}{30} = -\dfrac{1}{20}$
$\dfrac{1}{v_1} = \dfrac{1}{30} - \dfrac{1}{20} = -\dfrac{1}{60}$
$v_1 = -60 \text{ cm}$
The first image $I_1$ is formed $60 \text{ cm}$ in front of $M_1$.

Now, consider the second reflection at $M_2$:
The image $I_1$ acts as a virtual object for $M_2$. Since $I_1$ is $60 \text{ cm}$ from $M_1$ and the mirrors are separated by $d$, $I_1$ is located at a distance of $(60 - d)$ behind $M_2$.
Thus, the object distance for $M_2$ is $u_2 = +(60 - d)$.

The final image is formed at the position of the source $S$ itself, which is at a distance of $(d - 30)$ in front of $M_2$.
Thus, the image distance for $M_2$ is $v_2 = -(d - 30)$.

Using the mirror formula for $M_2$:
$\dfrac{1}{v_2} + \dfrac{1}{u_2} = \dfrac{1}{f_2}$
$\dfrac{1}{-(d - 30)} + \dfrac{1}{60 - d} = \dfrac{1}{20}$
$\dfrac{-(60 - d) + (d - 30)}{(d - 30)(60 - d)} = \dfrac{1}{20}$
$\dfrac{2d - 90}{90d - d^2 - 1800} = \dfrac{1}{20}$

Cross-multiplying yields:
$40d - 1800 = 90d - d^2 - 1800$
$d^2 - 50d = 0$
$d(d - 50) = 0$

Since $d \neq 0$, we get $d = 50 \text{ cm}$.
The distance separating the two mirrors is $50 \text{ cm}$.

Answer: $50 \text{ cm}$

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: A converging mirror $M_1$, a point source $S$, and a diverging mirror $M_2$ are configured. The source is located at a distance of $30 \text{ cm}$ from $M_1$. Each mirror has a focal length of $20 \text{ cm}$. Taking into account only the images produced by at most two reflections, it is observed that one image coincides with the source itself. Determine the location of the image formed by a single reflection from $M_2$.
options: $20 \text{ cm}$ from the diverging mirror closer to the converging mirror
$20 \text{ cm}$ from the diverging mirror farther from the converging mirror
$10 \text{ cm}$ from the diverging mirror farther from the converging mirror
$10 \text{ cm}$ from the diverging mirror closer to the converging mirror
questions.solution:
For the converging mirror $M_1$, the focal length is $f_1 = -20 \text{ cm}$ and the object distance is $u_1 = -30 \text{ cm}$.

Using the mirror formula for $M_1$:
$\dfrac{1}{v_1} + \dfrac{1}{u_1} = \dfrac{1}{f_1}$
$\dfrac{1}{v_1} - \dfrac{1}{30} = -\dfrac{1}{20} \Rightarrow v_1 = -60 \text{ cm}$

Let the distance between the source $S$ and the diverging mirror $M_2$ be $x$. The distance between the two mirrors is $d = 30 + x$.

For the image to coincide with the source after two reflections (first from $M_1$ and then from $M_2$), the image $I_1$ formed by $M_1$ acts as a virtual object for $M_2$.

The distance of $I_1$ from $M_2$ is $60 - d = 60 - (30 + x) = 30 - x$. Since it is formed behind $M_2$, the object distance for $M_2$ is $u_2 = +(30 - x)$.

The final image is formed at the source $S$, which is at a distance $x$ in front of $M_2$. Thus, the image distance for $M_2$ is $v_2 = -x$.

Using the mirror formula for $M_2$ ($f_2 = +20 \text{ cm}$):
$\dfrac{1}{v_2} + \dfrac{1}{u_2} = \dfrac{1}{f_2}$
$\dfrac{1}{-x} + \dfrac{1}{30 - x} = \dfrac{1}{20}$
$\dfrac{-30 + x + x}{-x(30 - x)} = \dfrac{1}{20}$
$\dfrac{2x - 30}{x^2 - 30x} = -\dfrac{1}{20}$
$-40x + 600 = x^2 - 30x$
$x^2 + 10x - 600 = 0$
$(x + 30)(x - 20) = 0$

Since distance cannot be negative, $x = 20 \text{ cm}$.

To find the location of the image formed by a single reflection from $M_2$, we use $u = -20 \text{ cm}$ and $f = +20 \text{ cm}$:
$\dfrac{1}{v} + \dfrac{1}{-20} = \dfrac{1}{20}$
$\dfrac{1}{v} = \dfrac{1}{20} + \dfrac{1}{20} = \dfrac{1}{10} \Rightarrow v = +10 \text{ cm}$

The positive sign indicates that the image is formed $10 \text{ cm}$ behind the diverging mirror $M_2$. Since $M_1$ is in front of $M_2$, the region behind $M_2$ is farther from the converging mirror.

Answer: $10 \text{ cm}$ from the diverging mirror farther from the converging mirror

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: A light ray strikes a clean slab of ice of thickness $1.00 \text{ m}$ at an angle of $45^{}^{{}^{\circ}}$ to the surface. It is then refracted into the ice at an angle of $30^{}^{{}^{\circ}}$. Determine the time taken by the light ray to cross the slab. The speed of light in vacuum is $3 \times 10^8 \text{ m s}^{-1}$.
questions.solution:
Angle of incidence, $i = 90^{}^{{}^{\circ}} - 45^{}^{{}^{\circ}} = 45^{}^{{}^{\circ}}$

Angle of refraction, $r = 30^{}^{{}^{\circ}}$

Refractive index of ice, $\mu = \dfrac{\sin i}{\sin r} = \dfrac{\sin 45^{}^{{}^{\circ}}}{\sin 30^{}^{{}^{\circ}}} = \dfrac{1/\sqrt{2}}{1/2} = \sqrt{2}$

Speed of light in ice, $v = \dfrac{c}{\mu} = \dfrac{3 \times 10^8}{\sqrt{2}} \text{ m s}^{-1}$

Distance travelled by light in the slab, $L = \dfrac{d}{\cos r} = \dfrac{1}{\cos 30^{}^{{}^{\circ}}} = \dfrac{2}{\sqrt{3}} \text{ m}$

Time taken, $t = \dfrac{L}{v} = \dfrac{2 / \sqrt{3}}{3 \times 10^8 / \sqrt{2}} = \dfrac{2\sqrt{2}}{3\sqrt{3}} \times 10^{-8} \text{ s}$

$t = \dfrac{2 \times 1.414}{3 \times 1.732} \times 10^{-8} \text{ s} \approx 5.44 \times 10^{-9} \text{ s}$

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: A $1.00 \text{ m}$ long pole stands half-dipped in a swimming pool where the water level is $50.0 \text{ cm}$ above the bed. The refractive index of the water is $1.33$, and sunlight strikes at an angle of $45^{}^{{}^{\circ}}$ with the vertical. Determine the length of the pole's shadow on the bed.
questions.solution:
The total length of the pole is $100 \text{ cm}$. Since it is half-dipped in the pool, the length of the pole above the water surface is $50 \text{ cm}$ and the length below the water surface is $50 \text{ cm}$.

The sunlight strikes at an angle of $45^{}^{{}^{\circ}}$ with the vertical. The shadow cast by the portion of the pole above the water on the water surface has a length $x_1$ given by:

$x_1 = 50 \tan 45^{}^{{}^{\circ}} = 50 \text{ cm}$

The light ray from the tip of the pole strikes the water surface at an angle of incidence $i = 45^{}^{{}^{\circ}}$. Let the angle of refraction be $r$. Applying Snell's law at the air-water interface:

$\sin i = \mu \sin r$

$\sin 45^{}^{{}^{\circ}} = 1.33 \sin r$

$\sin r = \dfrac{1}{1.33\sqrt{2}}$

Taking $\sqrt{2} \approx 1.41$, we get:

$\sin r \approx \dfrac{1}{1.33 \times 1.41} \approx 0.533$

The tangent of the angle of refraction is:

$\tan r = \dfrac{\sin r}{\sqrt{1 - \sin^2 r}} \approx \dfrac{0.533}{\sqrt{1 - (0.533)^2}} \approx 0.630$

The refracted ray travels a vertical depth of $50 \text{ cm}$ to reach the bed of the pool. The horizontal distance $x_2$ covered by the refracted ray in the water is:

$x_2 = 50 \tan r = 50 \times 0.630 = 31.5 \text{ cm}$

The total length of the pole's shadow on the bed is the sum of the horizontal distances:

$L = x_1 + x_2 = 50 + 31.5 = 81.5 \text{ cm}$

Answer: $81.5 \text{ cm}$

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: A small piece of wood floats on the surface of a $2.5 \text{ m}$ deep lake. Determine the position where the shadow forms on the bottom when the sun is just setting. The refractive index of water is $4/3$.
options: $1.42 \text{ m}$ shifted from the position directly below the piece of wood
$3.33 \text{ m}$ shifted from the position directly below the piece of wood
$2.83 \text{ m}$ shifted from the position directly below the piece of wood
$1.88 \text{ m}$ shifted from the position directly below the piece of wood
questions.solution:
When the sun is just setting, the angle of incidence of the light rays is $i = 90^{{}^{{}^{\circ}}}$.

Using Snell's law:

$\sin(90^{{}^{{}^{\circ}}}) = \mu \sin(r)$

$1 = \dfrac{4}{3} \sin(r) \Rightarrow \sin(r) = \dfrac{3}{4}$

The tangent of the angle of refraction is:

$\tan(r) = \dfrac{\sin(r)}{\sqrt{1 - \sin^2(r)}} = \dfrac{3/4}{\sqrt{1 - (3/4)^2}} = \dfrac{3}{\sqrt{7}}$

The horizontal shift of the shadow from the position directly below the piece of wood is:

$x = h \tan(r)$

Substituting $h = 2.5 \text{ m}$:

$x = 2.5 \times \dfrac{3}{\sqrt{7}} = \dfrac{7.5}{\sqrt{7}}$

Using $\sqrt{7} \approx 2.645$:

$x \approx \dfrac{7.5}{2.645} \approx 2.83 \text{ m}$

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: A microscope $M$ is focused on an object $P$. A glass slab having a thickness of $2.1 \text{ cm}$ and a refractive index of $1.5$ is inserted between $P$ and $M$. Determine the distance by which the microscope must be shifted to bring the object back into focus.
questions.solution:
When a glass slab of thickness $t$ and refractive index $\mu$ is inserted between an object and a microscope, the apparent shift of the object is given by:

$\Delta x = t \left($1 - $\dfrac{1}{\mu}\right)

Given $t = 2.1 $\text{ cm} and $\mu = 1.5 = $\dfrac{3}{2}, substituting these values into the formula gives:

\Delta$x = 2.1 \left(1 - \dfrac{2}{3}\right)$

$\Delta x = 2.1 \times \dfrac{1}{3}$

$\Delta x = 0.7 \text{ cm}$

The object appears to be shifted closer by $0.7 \text{ cm}$. Therefore, the microscope must be shifted by $0.7 \text{ cm}$ to bring the object back into focus.$

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: A vessel holds water up to a height of $20 \text{ cm}$, with an oil layer extending another $20 \text{ cm}$ above it. The refractive indices of the water and the oil are $1.33$ and $1.30$, respectively. Determine the apparent depth of the vessel when viewed from above.
questions.solution:
The apparent depth of a vessel with multiple immiscible liquid layers is given by the sum of the apparent depths of the individual layers.

$d_{app} = \dfrac{h_1}{\mu_1} + \dfrac{h_2}{\mu_2}$

Given values are:
$h_1 = 20 \text{ cm}$ (height of water)
$\mu_1 = 1.33$ (refractive index of water)
$h_2 = 20 \text{ cm}$ (height of oil)
$\mu_2 = 1.30$ (refractive index of oil)

Substituting the values into the formula:

$d_{app} = \dfrac{20}{1.33} + \dfrac{20}{1.30}$

$d_{app} \approx 15.04 \text{ cm} + 15.38 \text{ cm}$

$d_{app} \approx 30.42 \text{ cm}$

Rounding to one decimal place, the apparent depth is $30.4 \text{ cm}$.

questions.solution:
The apparent shift $\Delta x$ produced by a transparent slab of thickness $t$ and refractive index $\mu$ is given by $\Delta x = t \left(1 - \dfrac{1}{\mu}\right)$.

For multiple slabs, the total shift is the sum of the individual shifts. The air gaps do not contribute to the shift as their refractive index is $1$.

$\Delta x = \dfrac{0.16}{1.4} + \dfrac{0.09}{1.3} + \dfrac{0.04}{1.2}$

Rounding to one decimal place, the total shift is approximately $0.2 \text{ cm}$.

Since the shift is in the direction of the incident light (upwards towards the observer), the image is formed $0.2 \text{ cm}$ above point $P$.

Answer: $0.2 \text{ cm}$ above $P$

questions.q: A stack of $k$ transparent slabs is arranged one on top of another, having refractive indices $\mu_1, \mu_2, \mu_3, \ldots, \mu_k$ and respective thicknesses $t_1, t_2, t_3, \ldots, t_k$. If an object is viewed through this assembly using nearly perpendicular light, determine the equivalent refractive index of the system that would cause the image to form at the identical location.
questions.solution:
The apparent depth of an object viewed through a single slab of thickness $t$ and refractive index $\mu$ is given by $\dfrac{t}{\mu}$.

For a stack of $k$ slabs, the total apparent depth is the sum of the individual apparent depths:

Apparent depth $= \sum_{i=1}^{k} \dfrac{t_i}{\mu_i}$

If the entire assembly is replaced by a single equivalent slab of total thickness $\sum_{i=1}^{k} t_i$ and equivalent refractive index $\mu_{eq}$, its apparent depth would be:

Equivalent apparent depth $= \dfrac{\sum_{i=1}^{k} t_i}{\mu_{eq}}$

For the image to form at the identical location, the total apparent depth must be equal to the equivalent apparent depth:

$\dfrac{\sum_{i=1}^{k} t_i}{\mu_{eq}} = \sum_{i=1}^{k} \dfrac{t_i}{\mu_i}$

Rearranging the above equation to solve for $\mu_{eq}$, we get:

$\mu_{eq} = \dfrac{\sum_{i=1}^{k} t_i}{\sum_{i=1}^{k} \left(\dfrac{t_i}{\mu_i}\right)}$

questions.q: A cylindrical vessel with a diameter of $12\text{ cm}$ holds $800\pi \text{ cm}^3$ of water. A cylindrical glass piece having a diameter of $8.0 \text{ cm}$ and a height of $8.0 \text{ cm}$ is placed inside the vessel. Determine the position of the image of the vessel's bottom under the glass piece, when viewed by paraxial rays from above, as shown in the figure. The refractive index of glass is $1.50$ and that of water is $1.33$.
questions.solution:
Volume of water initially in the vessel, $V_w = 800\pi \text{ cm}^3$.

Radius of the cylindrical vessel, $R = \dfrac{12}{2} = 6 \text{ cm}$.

Radius of the glass piece, $r = \dfrac{8.0}{2} = 4.0 \text{ cm}$.

Height of the glass piece, $h_g = 8.0 \text{ cm}$.

Volume of the glass piece, $V_g = \pi r^2 h_g = \pi (4)^2 (8) = 128\pi \text{ cm}^3$.

When the glass piece is placed in the vessel, it sinks to the bottom. The total volume occupied up to the new water level $H$ is:
$V_{\text{total}} = V_w + V_g = 800\pi + 128\pi = 928\pi \text{ cm}^3$.

The new height of the water level from the bottom is:
$H = \dfrac{V_{\text{total}}}{\pi R^2} = \dfrac{928\pi}{\pi (6)^2} = \dfrac{928}{36} = \dfrac{232}{9} \text{ cm}$.

The thickness of the water layer above the glass piece is:
$h_w = H - h_g = \dfrac{232}{9} - 8 = \dfrac{160}{9} \text{ cm}$.

When viewed from above, the apparent shift of the bottom of the vessel is the sum of the shifts produced by the glass piece and the water layer.
Apparent shift, $\Delta x = h_g \left(1 - \dfrac{1}{\mu_g}\right) + h_w \left(1 - \dfrac{1}{\mu_w}\right)$

Substituting $\mu_g = 1.5 = \dfrac{3}{2}$ and $\mu_w = 1.33 \approx \dfrac{4}{3}$:
$\Delta x = 8 \left(1 - \dfrac{2}{3}\right) + \dfrac{160}{9} \left(1 - \dfrac{3}{4}\right)$

$\Delta x = 8 \left(\dfrac{1}{3}\right) + \dfrac{160}{9} \left(\dfrac{1}{4}\right)$

$\Delta x = \dfrac{8}{3} + \dfrac{40}{9} = \dfrac{24 + 40}{9} = \dfrac{64}{9} \text{ cm}$

$\Delta x \approx 7.11 \text{ cm}$

Therefore, the image of the bottom is formed $7.1 \text{ cm}$ above the actual bottom.

Answer: $7.1 \text{ cm}$ above the bottom

questions.q: Observe the setup illustrated in the figure. The base of the pot functions as a reflecting plane mirror, while S represents a small fish and T represents a human eye. The refractive index of the water is $\mu$. Determine the distance(s) from itself at which the eye observes the image(s) of the fish.
questions.solution:
The eye observes two images of the fish: one formed by direct light rays and the other formed by rays reflected from the mirror at the base.

For the direct image, the real depth of the fish from the water surface is $H - \dfrac{H}{2} = \dfrac{H}{2}$.

The apparent depth of this image from the water surface is $d_1 = \dfrac{H}{2\mu}$.

The distance of this first image from the eye is $D_1 = H + d_1 = H + \dfrac{H}{2\mu} = H\left(1 + \dfrac{1}{2\mu}\right)$ below the eye.

For the reflected image, the fish is at a distance of $\dfrac{H}{2}$ above the plane mirror at the base.

The mirror forms a virtual image of the fish at a distance of $\dfrac{H}{2}$ below the base.

The real depth of this reflected image from the water surface is $H + \dfrac{H}{2} = \dfrac{3H}{2}$.

The apparent depth of this reflected image from the water surface is $d_2 = \dfrac{3H}{2\mu}$.

The distance of this second image from the eye is $D_2 = H + d_2 = H + \dfrac{3H}{2\mu} = H\left(1 + \dfrac{3}{2\mu}\right)$ below the eye.

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: A small object is located at the centre of the bottom of a cylindrical vessel of radius $3 \text{ cm}$ and height $4 \text{ cm}$, which is completely filled with water. Consider a ray that leaves the vessel through a corner. Suppose this ray, along with the ray travelling along the axis of the vessel, is used to trace the image. Determine the apparent depth of the image and the ratio of the real depth to the apparent depth under these assumptions. The refractive index of water is $1.33$.
questions.solution:
Let the real depth of the vessel be $H = 4 \text{ cm}$ and its radius be $R = 3 \text{ cm}$.

The object is at the centre of the bottom. A ray travelling from the object to the corner of the vessel has an angle of incidence $i$ at the water surface. From the geometry of the vessel:

$\tan i = \dfrac{R}{H} = \dfrac{3}{4}$

This gives $\sin i = \dfrac{3}{5}$.

Applying Snell's law at the corner of the vessel:

$n \sin i = 1 \cdot \sin r$

$\dfrac{4}{3} \times \dfrac{3}{5} = \sin r$

$\sin r = \dfrac{4}{5}$

This implies $\tan r = \dfrac{4}{3}$.

The refracted ray emerges at an angle $r$ with the normal. When this ray is traced backward, it intersects the normal (the axis of the vessel) at the apparent depth $h'$. From the geometry of the backward-traced ray:

$\tan r = \dfrac{R}{h'}$

$\dfrac{4}{3} = \dfrac{3}{h'}$

$h' = \dfrac{9}{4} = 2.25 \text{ cm}$

The ratio of the real depth to the apparent depth under these assumptions is:

$\text{Ratio} = \dfrac{H}{h'} = \dfrac{4}{2.25} = \dfrac{16}{9} \approx 1.78$

questions.q: A cylindrical vessel, having both its diameter and height equal to $30 \text{ cm}$, rests on a horizontal surface. A small particle $P$ is located inside it at a distance of $5.0 \text{ cm}$ from the centre. An eye is situated such that the edge of the bottom is just visible, as shown in the figure. The particle $P$ lies in the plane of the drawing. Determine the minimum height to which water must be poured into the vessel so that the particle $P$ becomes visible.

Let the bottom-left corner of the vessel be the origin $(0,0)$. The top-right corner is at $(30, 30)$.

questions.q: A light ray strikes a $\sqrt{2} \text{ cm}$ thick plate ($\mu = 2.0$) at an angle of $45^{}^{{}^{\circ}}$ relative to the normal. Determine the shift in the path of the light as it emerges from the plate.
questions.solution:
Using Snell's law at the first interface:

$\sin i = \mu \sin r$

$\sin 45^\circ = 2.0 \sin r$

$\dfrac{1}{\sqrt{2}} = 2 \sin r \Rightarrow \sin r = \dfrac{1}{2\sqrt{2}}$

From this, we find $\cos r$:

$\cos r = \sqrt{1 - \sin^2 r} = \sqrt{1 - \dfrac{1}{8}} = \dfrac{\sqrt{7}}{2\sqrt{2}}$

The lateral shift $x$ of the emergent ray is given by:

$x = \dfrac{t \sin(i - r)}{\cos r} = t (\sin i - \cos i \tan r)$

Substituting the values:

$x = \sqrt{2} \left( \sin 45^\circ - \cos 45^\circ $\dfrac{\sin r}{\cos r} \right)

$x = $\sqrt{2} \left( \dfrac{1}{\sqrt{2}} - \dfrac{1}{\sqrt{2}} \dfrac{1 / (2\sqrt{2})}{\sqrt{7} / (2\sqrt{2})} \right)$

$x = \sqrt{2} \left( $\dfrac{1}{\sqrt{2}} - \dfrac{1}{\sqrt{2}} \dfrac{1}{\sqrt{7}} \right)

$x = 1 - $\dfrac{1}{\sqrt{7}}

Using \sqrt{7} \approx$2.645$:

$x = 1 - $\dfrac{1}{2.645} \approx$1 - 0.378 = 0.622 \text{ cm}$

questions.q: An optical fibre ($\mu = 1.72$) is enclosed by a glass coating ($\mu = 1.50$). Determine the critical angle for total internal reflection at the fibre-glass interface.
questions.solution:
The critical angle $\theta_c$ for total internal reflection at the interface of two media is given by $\sin \theta_c = \dfrac{\mu_2}{\mu_1}$, where $\mu_2$ is the refractive index of the rarer medium and $\mu_1$ is the refractive index of the denser medium.

Given $\mu_1 = 1.72$ (optical fibre) and $\mu_2 = 1.50$ (glass coating).

Substituting the values:

$\sin \theta_c = \dfrac{1.50}{1.72}$

$\sin \theta_c = \dfrac{150}{172}$

$\sin \theta_c = \dfrac{75}{86}$

$\theta_c = \sin^{-1} \left(\dfrac{75}{86}\right)$

questions.q: A light ray strikes the face $AB$ of a right-angled prism $ABC$ ($\mu = 1.50$) normally, as depicted in the figure. Determine the maximum value of the angle $\phi$ for which the light ray is totally internally reflected at the surface $AC$.
questions.solution:
When the light ray strikes the face $AB$ normally, it enters the prism undeviated and travels parallel to the base $BC$.

At the surface $AC$, the angle between the incident horizontal ray and the surface $AC$ is $\phi$.

Therefore, the angle of incidence $i$ at the surface $AC$ is given by:

$i = 90^{\circ} - \phi$

For total internal reflection to occur at the surface $AC$, the angle of incidence must be greater than or equal to the critical angle $\theta_c$ of the prism:

$i \ge \theta_c$

$90^{\circ} - \phi \ge \theta_c$

$\phi \le 90^{\circ} - \theta_c$

The maximum value of $\phi$ is:

$\phi_{\text{max}} = 90^{\circ} - \theta_c$

Taking the cosine of both sides, we get:

$\cos \phi_{\text{max}} = \cos(90^{\circ} - \theta_c) = \sin \theta_c$

We know that the critical angle is given by $\sin \theta_c = \dfrac{1}{\mu}$.

Given $\mu = 1.50 = \dfrac{3}{2}$, we have:

$\sin \theta_c = \dfrac{1}{1.50} = \dfrac{2}{3}$

Substituting this value, we get:

$\cos \phi_{\text{max}} = \dfrac{2}{3}$

$\phi_{\text{max}} = \cos^{-1}\left(\dfrac{2}{3}\right)$

questions.q: Determine the maximum angle of refraction when a light ray is refracted from glass ($\mu = 1.50$) into air.
questions.solution:
According to Snell's law:

$\mu_1 \sin i = \mu_2 \sin r$

For light traveling from glass ($\mu_1 = 1.50$) to air ($\mu_2 = 1$), we have:

$1.50 \sin i = 1 \sin r$

The maximum possible value for $\sin r$ during refraction is $1$, which occurs when the incident angle is equal to the critical angle.

When $\sin r = 1$, the angle of refraction is $r = 90^{}^{{}^{\circ}}$.

Therefore, the maximum angle of refraction is $90^{}^{{}^{\circ}}$.

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: Light is incident from glass ($\mu = 1.5$) to air. Which of the following best describes the variation of the angle of deviation $\delta$ with the angle of incidence $i$ for $0 < i < 90^{}^{{}^{\circ}}$?
options: $\delta$ increases non-linearly for $i < i_c$, is continuous at $i = i_c$, and decreases linearly for $i > i_c$.
$\delta$ increases continuously for all $0 < i < 90^{}^{{}^{\circ}}$ without any sudden jump at the critical angle $i_c$.
$\delta$ increases non-linearly for $i < i_c$, jumps discontinuously at $i = i_c$, and decreases linearly for $i > i_c$.
$\delta$ increases linearly for $i < i_c$, jumps discontinuously at $i = i_c$, and decreases non-linearly for $i > i_c$.
questions.solution:
For $i < i_c$, refraction takes place.

By Snell's law, $\mu \sin i = 1 \cdot \sin r \Rightarrow r = \sin^{-1}(\mu \sin i)$

The angle of deviation is $\delta = r - i = \sin^{-1}(\mu \sin i) - i$

This shows that $\delta$ increases non-linearly with $i$ for $i < i_c$.

At $i = i_c$, the angle of refraction is $r = 90^{}^{{}^{\circ}}$.

The deviation is $\delta_1 = 90^{}^{{}^{\circ}} - i_c$.

For $i > i_c$, total internal reflection takes place.

The angle of deviation for reflection is $\delta = 180^{}^{{}^{\circ}} - 2i$.

This shows that $\delta$ decreases linearly with $i$ for $i > i_c$.

Just after the critical angle, as $i \to i_c$, the deviation due to total internal reflection is $\delta_2 = 180^{}^{{}^{\circ}} - 2i_c$.

Since $\delta_2 \neq \delta_1$, there is a discontinuous jump in the angle of deviation at $i = i_c$.

Therefore, $\delta$ increases non-linearly for $i < i_c$, jumps discontinuously at $i = i_c$, and decreases linearly for $i > i_c$.

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: Light is incident from glass ($\mu = 1.50$) to water ($\mu = 1.33$). Determine the range of the angle of deviation for which there are two angles of incidence.
questions.solution:
The critical angle $\theta_c$ for light traveling from glass to water is given by:

$\sin \theta_c = \dfrac{\mu_w}{\mu_g} = \dfrac{4/3}{3/2} = \dfrac{8}{9}$

$\theta_c = \sin^{-1} $\$left(\dfrac{8}{9}\right)

When the angle of incidence $i$ is less than the critical angle ($0 \le i < \theta_c$), refraction occurs. The angle of deviation $\delta$ is given by $\delta = r - i$. As $i$ increases from $0$ to $\theta_c$, $r$ increases from $0$ to $\pi/2$. The deviation $\delta$ increases from $0$ to a maximum value of:

$\delta_1 = \dfrac{\pi}{2} - \theta_c$

When the angle of incidence $i$ is greater than or equal to the critical angle ($\theta_c \le i \le \pi/2$), total internal reflection (TIR) occurs. The angle of deviation is given by $\delta = \pi - 2i$. As $i$ increases from $\theta_c$ to $\pi/2$, the deviation $\delta$ decreases from a maximum of $\pi - 2\theta_c$ to $0$.

The range of deviation for refraction is $[0, \pi/2 - \theta_c)$ and for TIR is $[0, \pi - 2\theta_c]$. Since $\theta_c < \pi/2$, we have $\pi/2 - \theta_c < \pi - 2\theta_c$.

For a deviation $\delta$ to have two corresponding angles of incidence (one from refraction and one from TIR), it must lie in the overlapping range of both cases. This overlapping range is from $0$ to $\delta_1$.

The upper limit of this range is:

$\delta_1 = \dfrac{\pi}{2} - \sin^{-1} $\$left(\dfrac{8}{9}\right) = \cos^{-1}\left(\dfrac{8}{9}\right)

Thus, the range of the angle of deviation for which there are two angles of incidence is $0$ to $\cos^{-1} \left(\dfrac{8}{9}\right).$

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: Light is incident from glass ($\mu = 1.5$) into air. Determine the angle of incidence that results in an angle of deviation of $90^{}^{{}^{\circ}}$.
questions.solution:
The critical angle for the glass-air interface is given by $\sin \theta_c = \dfrac{1}{\mu} = \dfrac{1}{1.5} = \dfrac{2}{3}$.

For refraction, the angle of deviation is $\delta = r - i$. If $\delta = 90^{}^{{}^{\circ}}$, then $r = 90^{}^{{}^{\circ}} + i$, which is not possible since the maximum angle of refraction is $90^{}^{{}^{\circ}}$.

Therefore, the light must undergo total internal reflection. For total internal reflection, the angle of deviation is $\delta = 180^{}^{{}^{\circ}} - 2i$.

Given $\delta = 90^{}^{{}^{\circ}}$, we have:

$180^{}^{{}^{\circ}} - 2i = 90^{}^{{}^{\circ}}$

$2i = 90^{}^{{}^{\circ}} \Rightarrow i = 45^{}^{{}^{\circ}}$

We must verify if this angle is greater than the critical angle. Since $\sin 45^{}^{{}^{\circ}} = \dfrac{1}{\sqrt{2}} \approx 0.707$ and $\sin \theta_c = \dfrac{2}{3} \approx 0.667$, we have $i > \theta_c$.

Thus, total internal reflection occurs and the required angle of incidence is $45^{}^{{}^{\circ}}$.

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: A point source is located at a depth $h$ beneath the surface of water (refractive index $= \mu$). Identify the shape of the area on the water surface through which light escapes, along with the position of its centre.
options: A circular area with its centre directly above the point source
A rectangular area with its centre directly above the point source
A circular area whose centre is shifted horizontally by a distance $h$
An elliptical area with its centre directly above the point source
questions.solution:
Light rays from the point source at depth $h$ will escape the water surface if their angle of incidence at the water-air interface is less than or equal to the critical angle $\theta_c$.

The critical angle is given by $\sin \theta_c = \dfrac{1}{\mu}$.

By symmetry, the locus of all points on the surface where the angle of incidence is exactly $\theta_c$ is a circle.

The radius of this circle is $r = h \tan \theta_c = \dfrac{h}{\sqrt{\mu^2 - 1}}$.

Thus, the light escapes through a circular area on the water surface.

The centre of this circular area lies directly above the point source.

questions.q: A point source is located at a depth $h$ beneath the surface of water (refractive index $= \mu$). Light escapes through a circular area on the water surface. Determine the angle subtended by a radius of this area at the source.
questions.solution:
Light from the point source escapes the water surface only if the angle of incidence is less than or equal to the critical angle $\theta_c$.

The circular area is formed by the rays that strike the surface at an angle of incidence equal to the critical angle.

The angle subtended by the radius of this circular area at the source is exactly the critical angle $\theta_c$.

Using Snell's law for the critical angle, we have $\mu \sin \theta_c = 1 \times \sin 90^{{}^{{}^{\circ}}}$.

$\sin \theta_c = \dfrac{1}{\mu}$

$\theta_c = \sin^{-1} \left(\dfrac{1}{\mu}\right)$

questions.q: A container holds water up to a height of $20 \text{ cm}$ and a point source is situated at the centre of the container's bottom. A rubber ring of radius $15 \text{ cm}$ floats centrally on the water. The room's ceiling is $2.0 \text{ m}$ above the water surface. Determine the radius of the shadow of the ring formed on the ceiling. The refractive index of water is $4/3$.
questions.solution:
Let the angle of incidence of the light ray at the edge of the rubber ring be $i$.

From the geometry of the setup, we have:
$\tan i = \dfrac{r}{h} = \dfrac{15 \text{ cm}}{20 \text{ cm}} = \dfrac{3}{4}$

This gives $\sin i = \dfrac{3}{5}$.

Applying Snell's law at the water-air interface:
$\mu_{w} \sin i = \mu_{a} \sin r'$

$\dfrac{4}{3} \times \dfrac{3}{5} = 1 \times \sin r'$

$\sin r' = \dfrac{4}{5} \Rightarrow \tan r' = \dfrac{4}{3}$

The light ray emerges into the air at an angle $r'$ and travels to the ceiling, which is at a height $H = 2.0 \text{ m}$ above the water surface. The additional horizontal distance traveled by the ray in the air is:
$x = H \tan r' = 2.0 \times \dfrac{4}{3} = \dfrac{8}{3} \text{ m} \approx 2.667 \text{ m}$

The total radius of the shadow formed on the ceiling is the sum of the radius of the ring and the horizontal distance traveled in the air:
$R = r + x = 0.15 \text{ m} + 2.667 \text{ m} = 2.817 \text{ m}$

Rounding off to two decimal places, we get $R \approx 2.82 \text{ m}$.

questions.q: A container holds water up to a height of $20 \text{ cm}$ and a point source is situated at the centre of the container's bottom. A rubber ring of radius $r$ floats centrally on the water. The room's ceiling is $2.0 \text{ m}$ above the water surface. Determine the maximum value of $r$ for which the shadow of the ring is formed on the ceiling. The refractive index of water is $4/3$.
questions.solution:
For the shadow of the ring to be formed on the ceiling, the light rays from the point source passing just outside the ring must refract into the air and reach the ceiling.

This means the angle of incidence at the water surface must be less than or equal to the critical angle $\theta_c$. If the angle of incidence exceeds $\theta_c$, total internal reflection occurs and no light escapes to illuminate the ceiling outside the ring.

The critical angle is given by:

$\sin \theta_c = \dfrac{1}{\mu} = \dfrac{1}{4/3} = \dfrac{3}{4}$

From the geometry of the container, the maximum radius $r$ of the ring is related to the depth of the water $h$ by:

$\tan \theta_c = \dfrac{r}{h}$

Using $\sin \theta_c = \dfrac{3}{4}$, we find $\tan \theta_c$:

$\tan \theta_c = \dfrac{3}{\sqrt{4^2 - 3^2}} = \dfrac{3}{\sqrt{7}}$

Given $h = 20 \text{ cm}$, the maximum radius is:

$r = h \tan \theta_c = 20 \times \dfrac{3}{\sqrt{7}} = \dfrac{60}{\sqrt{7}} \text{ cm}$

Calculating the numerical value:

$r \approx \dfrac{60}{2.646} \approx 22.68 \text{ cm}$

Rounding to one decimal place, we get $22.7 \text{ cm}$.

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: Determine the angle of minimum deviation for an equilateral prism constructed from a material with a refractive index of $1.732$. What is the corresponding angle of incidence for this deviation?
questions.solution:
For an equilateral prism, the angle of the prism is $A = 60^{}^{{}^{\circ}}$.

The refractive index of the material is given as $\mu = 1.732 = \sqrt{3}$.

The relation between the refractive index, angle of prism, and angle of minimum deviation $\delta_m$ is:

$\mu = \dfrac{\sin\left(\dfrac{A + \delta_m}{2}\right)}{\sin\left(\dfrac{A}{2}\right)}$

Substituting the given values:

$\sqrt{3} = \dfrac{\sin\left(\dfrac{60^{}^{{}^{\circ}} + \delta_m}{2}\right)}{\sin\left(\dfrac{60^{}^{{}^{\circ}}}{2}\right)}$

$\sqrt{3} = \dfrac{\sin\left(30^{}^{{}^{\circ}} + \dfrac{\delta_m}{2}\right)}{\sin(30^{}^{{}^{\circ}})}$

$\sqrt{3} = \dfrac{\sin\left(30^{}^{{}^{\circ}} + \dfrac{\delta_m}{2}\right)}{\dfrac{1}{2}}$

$\sin\left(30^{}^{{}^{\circ}} + \dfrac{\delta_m}{2}\right) = \dfrac{\sqrt{3}}{2}$

Since $\sin(60^{}^{{}^{\circ}}) = \dfrac{\sqrt{3}}{2}$, we get:

$30^{}^{{}^{\circ}} + \dfrac{\delta_m}{2} = 60^{}^{{}^{\circ}}$

$\dfrac{\delta_m}{2} = 30^{}^{{}^{\circ}} \Rightarrow \delta_m = 60^{}^{{}^{\circ}}$

The corresponding angle of incidence $i$ at minimum deviation is given by:

$i = \dfrac{A + \delta_m}{2}$

$i = \dfrac{60^{}^{{}^{\circ}} + 60^{}^{{}^{\circ}}}{2} = 60^{}^{{}^{\circ}}$

Thus, the angle of minimum deviation is $60^{}^{{}^{\circ}}$ and the angle of incidence is $60^{}^{{}^{\circ}}$.

The light ray is incident normally on the first face of the prism, so the angle of incidence $i_1 = 0^\circ$ and the angle of refraction $r_1 = 0^\circ$.

For a prism, the refracting angle $A = r_1 + r_2$.

Applying Snell's law at the second face:

$\mu \sin(r_2) = \sin(e)$

Since the angles are small, $\sin(\theta) \approx \theta$:

$\mu r_2 = e$

$1.5 \times 4^\circ = e \Rightarrow e = 6^\circ$

The angle of deviation $\delta$ is:

$\delta = i_1 + e - A$

$\delta = 0^\circ + 6^\circ - 4^\circ = 2^\circ$

Alternatively, for a thin prism, the deviation is directly given by:

$\delta = (\mu - 1)A$

$\delta = (1.5 - 1) \times 4^\circ = 2^\circ$

questions.q: A light ray passing through a prism having a prism angle of $60^{}^{{}^{\circ}}$ is observed to deviate by $30^{}^{{}^{\circ}}$. What limit can be placed on the refractive index based on this data?
questions.solution:
The minimum deviation $\delta_\min$ for a prism is always less than or equal to any observed deviation $\delta$.

Given the prism angle $A = 60^{}^{{}^{\circ}}$ and an observed deviation $\delta = 30^{}^{{}^{\circ}}$, we have $\delta_\min \leq 30^{}^{{}^{\circ}}$.

The refractive index of the material of the prism is given by:

$\mu = \dfrac{\sin\left(\dfrac{A + \delta_\min}{2}\right)}{\sin\left(\dfrac{A}{2}\right)}$

Since $\delta_\min \leq 30^{}^{{}^{\circ}}$ and the sine function is increasing in this interval:

$\mu \leq \dfrac{\sin\left(\dfrac{60^{}^{{}^{\circ}} + 30^{}^{{}^{\circ}}}{2}\right)}{\sin\left(\dfrac{60^{}^{{}^{\circ}}}{2}\right)}$

$\mu \leq \sqrt{2}$

$v = -100 \text{ cm}$

$\dfrac{\mu_2}{v} - \dfrac{\mu_1}{u} = \dfrac{\mu_2 - \mu_1}{R}$

Substituting the given values:
$\dfrac{1.5}{v} - \dfrac{1.0}{-25} = \dfrac{1.5 - 1.0}{+20}$

$\dfrac{1.5}{v} + \dfrac{1}{25} = \dfrac{0.5}{20}$

$\dfrac{1.5}{v} = \dfrac{5 - 8}{200}$

questions.q: Two transparent media $A$ and $B$, having refractive indices $1.33$ and $1.48$ respectively, are separated by a spherical surface of radius $30 \text{ cm}$. Medium $A$ lies on the convex side of this surface. At what distance from the separating surface should a point object be positioned in medium $A$ to ensure that paraxial rays emerge parallel following refraction at the surface?
questions.solution:
For refraction at a single spherical surface, the formula is given by:

$\dfrac{n_2}{v} - \dfrac{n_1}{u} = \dfrac{n_2 - n_1}{R}$

Given that the object is in medium $A$, $n_1 = 1.33$ and $n_2 = 1.48$.

Since medium $A$ lies on the convex side of the surface, the surface is convex towards the incident light. Therefore, the center of curvature lies in medium $B$, making the radius of curvature positive: $R = +30 \text{ cm}$.

The paraxial rays emerge parallel after refraction, which means the image is formed at infinity, so $v = \infty$.

Substituting the values into the formula:

$\dfrac{1.48}{\infty} - \dfrac{1.33}{u} = \dfrac{1.48 - 1.33}{30}$

$0 - \dfrac{1.33}{u} = \dfrac{0.15}{30}$

$-\dfrac{1.33}{u} = \dfrac{1}{200}$

$u = -1.33 \times 200 = -266 \text{ cm}$

The negative sign indicates that the object is placed in front of the refracting surface. The distance of the object from the surface is $266.0 \text{ cm}$.

questions.q: A small object is embedded inside a glass sphere ($\mu = 1.5$) of radius $5.0 \text{ cm}$, located at a distance of $1.5 \text{ cm}$ left to the centre. Determine the position of the image of the object as seen by an observer standing to the left of the sphere.
questions.solution:
The formula for refraction at a single spherical surface is:

$\dfrac{\mu_2}{v} - \dfrac{\mu_1}{u} = \dfrac{\mu_2 - \mu_1}{R}$

The observer is to the left of the sphere, so the refraction occurs at the left surface. Let the pole be at the left surface. Taking the direction of incident light (from right to left) as positive, distances to the right of the pole are taken as negative.

Refractive index of the medium of the object (glass), $\mu_1 = 1.5$

Refractive index of the medium of the observer (air), $\mu_2 = 1$

The radius of the sphere is $5.0 \text{ cm}$. The centre of curvature is to the right of the pole, so $R = -5.0 \text{ cm}$.

The object is $1.5 \text{ cm}$ to the left of the centre. The position of the object from the pole is $u = -5.0 + 1.5 = -3.5 \text{ cm}$.

Substituting the values into the refraction formula:

$\dfrac{1}{v} - \dfrac{1.5}{-3.5} = \dfrac{1 - 1.5}{-5.0}$

$\dfrac{1}{v} + \dfrac{3}{7} = \dfrac{-0.5}{-5.0}$

$\dfrac{1}{v} + \dfrac{3}{7} = \dfrac{1}{10}$

$\dfrac{1}{v} = \dfrac{1}{10} - \dfrac{3}{7} = \dfrac{7 - 30}{70} = -\dfrac{23}{70}$

$v = -\dfrac{70}{23} \approx -3.04 \text{ cm}$

The negative sign indicates that the image is formed $3.04 \text{ cm}$ to the right of the left surface.

The distance of the image from the centre of the sphere is $5.0 - 3.04 = 1.96 \text{ cm}$.

Since the image is between the left surface and the centre, its position is $1.96 \text{ cm} \approx 2 \text{ cm}$ to the left of the centre.

questions.q: A small object is embedded inside a glass sphere ($\mu = 1.5$) of radius $5.0 \text{ cm}$, located at a distance of $1.5 \text{ cm}$ left to the centre. Determine the position of the image of the object as seen by an observer standing to the right of the sphere.
questions.solution:
The observer is to the right of the sphere, so refraction occurs at the right surface. Light travels from left to right, which is taken as the positive direction.

Let the pole $P$ be the rightmost point of the sphere.

Radius of curvature of the right surface is $R = -5.0 \text{ cm}$.

The object is $1.5 \text{ cm}$ to the left of the centre, so its distance from the pole $P$ is $u = -(5.0 + 1.5) = -6.5 \text{ cm}$.

Refractive index of the glass sphere is $\mu_1 = 1.5$ and for air is $\mu_2 = 1$.

Using the spherical refraction formula:

$\dfrac{\mu_2}{v} - \dfrac{\mu_1}{u} = \dfrac{\mu_2 - \mu_1}{R}$

$\dfrac{1}{v} - \dfrac{1.5}{-6.5} = \dfrac{1 - 1.5}{-5.0}$

$\dfrac{1}{v} + \dfrac{3}{13} = \dfrac{-0.5}{-5.0}$

$\dfrac{1}{v} + \dfrac{3}{13} = \dfrac{1}{10}$

$\dfrac{1}{v} = \dfrac{1}{10} - \dfrac{3}{13} = \dfrac{13 - 30}{130} = -\dfrac{17}{130}$

$v = -\dfrac{130}{17} \approx -7.65 \text{ cm}$

The negative sign indicates that the image is formed $7.65 \text{ cm}$ to the left of the right surface (pole $P$).

The distance of the image from the centre of the sphere is $7.65 - 5.0 = 2.65 \text{ cm}$.

Since the image is $7.65 \text{ cm}$ left of the pole and the centre is $5.0 \text{ cm}$ left of the pole, the image is $2.65 \text{ cm}$ left of the centre.

questions.q: A biconvex thick lens is made of glass ($\mu = 1.50$). Both of the surfaces have a radius of $10 \text{ cm}$, and the central thickness is $5 \text{ cm}$. Determine the location of the image for an object situated far away from the lens.
options: $11.1 \text{ cm}$ from the farther surface on the other side of the lens
$10.0 \text{ cm}$ from the farther surface on the other side of the lens
$10.8 \text{ cm}$ from the farther surface on the other side of the lens
$9.1 \text{ cm}$ from the farther surface on the other side of the lens
questions.solution:
For the first surface, using the formula for refraction at a spherical surface:

$\dfrac{\mu_2}{v_1} - \dfrac{\mu_1}{u} = \dfrac{\mu_2 - \mu_1}{R_1}$

Given $\mu_1 = 1$, $\mu_2 = 1.5$, $u = -\infty$, and $R_1 = +10 \text{ cm}$:

$\dfrac{1.5}{v_1} - 0 = \dfrac{1.5 - 1}{10}$

$\dfrac{1.5}{v_1} = \dfrac{0.5}{10} \Rightarrow v_1 = 30 \text{ cm}$

The image formed by the first surface acts as a virtual object for the second surface. The object distance for the second surface is:

$u_2 = v_1 - t = 30 - 5 = +25 \text{ cm}$

For the second surface, light travels from glass to air. Using $\mu_1 = 1.5$, $\mu_2 = 1$, and $R_2 = -10 \text{ cm}$:

$\dfrac{\mu_2}{v_2} - \dfrac{\mu_1}{u_2} = \dfrac{\mu_2 - \mu_1}{R_2}$

$\dfrac{1}{v_2} - \dfrac{1.5}{25} = \dfrac{1 - 1.5}{-10}$

$\dfrac{1}{v_2} - \dfrac{3}{50} = \dfrac{-0.5}{-10} = \dfrac{1}{20}$

$\dfrac{1}{v_2} = \dfrac{1}{20} + \dfrac{3}{50} = \dfrac{5 + 6}{100} = \dfrac{11}{100}$

$v_2 = \dfrac{100}{11} \approx 9.1 \text{ cm}$

The final image is formed at $9.1 \text{ cm}$ from the farther surface on the other side of the lens.

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: A narrow pencil of parallel light falls normally on a solid transparent sphere of radius $r$. Determine the required refractive index if the pencil is to be focused at the surface of the sphere.
questions.solution:
For refraction at a single spherical surface, the formula is $\dfrac{\mu_2}{v} - \dfrac{\mu_1}{u} = \dfrac{\mu_2 - \mu_1}{R}$.

Here, the incident light is a parallel pencil of rays, so $u = -\infty$. The light enters from air ($\mu_1 = 1$) into the transparent sphere ($\mu_2 = \mu$). The radius of curvature of the first surface is $R = +r$.

Substituting these values into the formula:

$\dfrac{\mu}{v} - \dfrac{1}{-\infty} = \dfrac{\mu - 1}{r}$

$\dfrac{\mu}{v} = \dfrac{\mu - 1}{r}$

$v = \dfrac{\mu r}{\mu - 1}$

For the rays to be focused at the opposite surface of the sphere, the image distance $v$ from the first surface must be equal to the diameter of the sphere, which is $2r$.

Equating the two expressions for $v$:

$\dfrac{\mu r}{\mu - 1} = 2r$

$\mu = 2(\mu - 1)$

$\mu = 2\mu - 2$

$\mu = 2$

questions.q: A narrow pencil of parallel light falls normally on a solid transparent sphere of radius $r$. Determine the required refractive index if the pencil is to be focused at the centre of the sphere.
questions.solution:
For refraction at the first spherical surface, the formula is $\dfrac{\mu_2}{v} - \dfrac{\mu_1}{u} = \dfrac{\mu_2 - \mu_1}{R}$.

Here, the light is incident from air ($\mu_1 = 1$) to the transparent sphere ($\mu_2 = \mu$).

Since the incident light is a parallel pencil, the object distance is $u = -\infty$.

The radius of curvature of the surface is $R = +r$.

The light is to be focused at the centre of the sphere, which is at a distance $r$ from the pole of the first surface. So, the image distance is $v = +r$.

Substituting these values into the refraction formula:

$\dfrac{\mu}{r} - \dfrac{1}{-\infty} = \dfrac{\mu - 1}{r}$

$\dfrac{\mu}{r} - 0 = \dfrac{\mu - 1}{r}$

$\mu = \mu - 1$

$0 = -1$

This leads to a mathematical contradiction, which implies that no such refractive index exists.

Conceptually, any ray passing through the centre of a sphere must travel along the normal to the surface. For a parallel beam, only the central axial ray is normal to the surface. All other parallel rays will have a non-zero angle of incidence and will be refracted at a non-zero angle of refraction, meaning they will deviate from the normal and miss the centre. Thus, it is not possible to focus a parallel pencil of light at the centre of the sphere.

questions.q: A cylindrical glass rod ($\mu = 1.5$) with a radius of $1.0 \text{ cm}$ has one end rounded into a hemispherical shape. This rod is submerged in water ($\mu = 4/3$). An object is positioned in the water on the axis of the rod, $8.0 \text{ cm}$ away from the rounded edge. Determine the location of the image of the object.
questions.solution:
Using the formula for refraction at a single spherical surface:

$\dfrac{\mu_2}{v} - \dfrac{\mu_1}{u} = \dfrac{\mu_2 - \mu_1}{R}$

Given:
Refractive index of the surrounding medium (water), $\mu_1 = \dfrac{4}{3}$
Refractive index of the rod (glass), $\mu_2 = 1.5 = \dfrac{3}{2}$
Object distance, $u = -8.0 \text{ cm}$
Radius of curvature, $R = +1.0 \text{ cm}$ (positive since the center of curvature lies in the direction of incident light)

Substituting the values into the formula:

$\dfrac{3/2}{v} - \dfrac{4/3}{-8.0} = \dfrac{3/2 - 4/3}{1.0}$

$\dfrac{3}{2v} + \dfrac{4}{24} = \dfrac{9/6 - 8/6}{1}$

$\dfrac{3}{2v} + \dfrac{1}{6} = \dfrac{1}{6}$

$\dfrac{3}{2v} = 0$

$v = \infty$

The image is formed at infinity.

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: A paperweight ($\mu = 1.5$) shaped as a hemisphere of radius $3.0 \text{ cm}$ is placed to hold down a printed page. An observer views the page vertically through the paperweight. At what height above the page will the printed letters near the centre appear to the observer?
questions.solution:
For refraction at a spherical surface, the formula is:

$\dfrac{\mu_2}{v} - \dfrac{\mu_1}{u} = \dfrac{\mu_2 - \mu_1}{R}$

Here, light travels from the glass paperweight to the air. Therefore, the refractive index of the first medium is $\mu_1 = 1.5$ and the second medium is $\mu_2 = 1.0$.

The printed letters are located at the center of the flat surface, which is also the center of curvature of the spherical surface. Taking the pole of the spherical surface as the origin and the downward direction as negative, we have:

$u = -3.0 \text{ cm}$

$R = -3.0 \text{ cm}$

Substituting these values into the formula:

$\dfrac{1}{v} - \dfrac{1.5}{-3.0} = \dfrac{1.0 - 1.5}{-3.0}$

$\dfrac{1}{v} + 0.5 = \dfrac{-0.5}{-3.0}$

$\dfrac{1}{v} + \dfrac{1}{2} = \dfrac{1}{6}$

$\dfrac{1}{v} = \dfrac{1}{6} - \dfrac{1}{2} = -\dfrac{1}{3}$

$v = -3.0 \text{ cm}$

The image is formed at a distance of $3.0 \text{ cm}$ below the pole, which is exactly the original position of the printed page.

Conceptually, the light rays originating from the center of curvature strike the spherical surface normally and pass into the air undeviated. Thus, they appear to come from the object itself.

Since the image is formed at the object's exact location, the apparent shift is zero. Therefore, the letters appear at a height of $0 \text{ cm}$ above the page.

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: A paperweight ($\mu = 1.5$) in the shape of a hemisphere of radius $3.0 \text{ cm}$ is placed to hold down a printed page. The paperweight is inverted in its place such that the spherical surface touches the paper. An observer views the page vertically through the paperweight. Determine the height above the page at which the printed letters near the centre appear to the observer.
questions.solution:
The paperweight is inverted, which means its flat surface is horizontal at the top and the spherical surface touches the page at the bottom.

For the letters near the center of the page, they are virtually in contact with the pole of the spherical surface. Thus, the real depth of these letters from the top flat surface is equal to the radius of the hemisphere, $R = 3.0 \text{ cm}$.

When the observer views the letters vertically from above, refraction occurs at the top flat surface. The apparent depth $d'$ of the letters from the top surface is given by:

$d' = \dfrac{R}{\mu}$

Substituting the given values:

$d' = \dfrac{3.0}{1.5} = 2.0 \text{ cm}$

The image of the letters is formed $2.0 \text{ cm}$ below the top flat surface.

Since the top flat surface is at a height of $3.0 \text{ cm}$ from the page, the apparent height of the letters above the page is:

$h = 3.0 \text{ cm} - 2.0 \text{ cm} = 1.0 \text{ cm}$

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: A hemispherical section of the surface of a solid glass sphere ($\mu = 1.5$) of radius $r$ is silvered to render the inner side reflecting. An object is positioned on the axis of the hemisphere at a distance $3r$ from the centre of the sphere. Light from the object is refracted at the unsilvered part, subsequently reflected from the silvered part, and refracted again at the unsilvered part. Locate the final image formed.
options: At the reflecting surface of the sphere
Midway between the centre and the reflecting surface
At the unsilvered surface of the sphere
At the centre of the sphere
questions.solution:
Let the pole of the unsilvered surface be $P_1$ and the pole of the silvered surface be $P_2$. The distance between $P_1$ and $P_2$ is the diameter of the sphere, $2r$.

The object $O$ is at a distance $3r$ from the centre $C$, which means it is at a distance $3r - r = 2r$ from $P_1$.

For the first refraction at the unsilvered surface $P_1$:
Object distance, $u = -2r$
Radius of curvature, $R = +r$
Refractive indices, $\mu_1 = 1$ (air) and $\mu_2 = 1.5$ (glass)

Using the spherical refraction formula:
$\dfrac{\mu_2}{v_1} - \dfrac{\mu_1}{u} = \dfrac{\mu_2 - \mu_1}{R}$

$\dfrac{1.5}{v_1} - \dfrac{1}{-2r} = \dfrac{1.5 - 1}{r}$

$\dfrac{1.5}{v_1} + \dfrac{1}{2r} = \dfrac{0.5}{r} = \dfrac{1}{2r}$

$\dfrac{1.5}{v_1} = 0 \Rightarrow v_1 = \infty$
The refracted rays become parallel to the principal axis.

For the reflection at the silvered surface $P_2$:
The parallel rays fall on the concave mirror formed by the silvered surface. The radius of curvature of this mirror is $r$, so its focal length is $f = \dfrac{r}{2}$.
Parallel rays converge at the focus, so the reflected image $I_2$ is formed at a distance $\dfrac{r}{2}$ from $P_2$.
The distance of $I_2$ from the unsilvered surface $P_1$ is $2r - \dfrac{r}{2} = 1.5r$.

For the second refraction at the unsilvered surface $P_1$:
The object is now $I_2$, so $u = -1.5r$.
Light travels from glass to air, so $\mu_1 = 1.5$ and $\mu_2 = 1$.
The radius of curvature is $R = -r$ (since the centre of curvature is on the side from which light is coming).

Using the refraction formula again:
$\dfrac{1}{v_3} - \dfrac{1.5}{-1.5r} = \dfrac{1 - 1.5}{-r}$

$\dfrac{1}{v_3} + \dfrac{1}{r} = \dfrac{0.5}{r}$

$\dfrac{1}{v_3} = \dfrac{0.5}{r} - \dfrac{1}{r} = -\dfrac{0.5}{r} = -\dfrac{1}{2r}$

$v_3 = -2r$

The negative sign indicates that the final image is formed at a distance $2r$ from $P_1$ on the same side as the incident light (inside the sphere). Since the diameter of the sphere is $2r$, this position corresponds exactly to the pole $P_2$.

Thus, the final image is formed at the reflecting surface of the sphere.

Answer: At the reflecting surface of the sphere

questions.q: A thin concavo-convex glass lens (refractive index $1.5$) features a convex surface with a $20 \text{ cm}$ radius of curvature and a concave surface with a $60 \text{ cm}$ radius of curvature. The convex side is silvered and rests on a horizontal surface. A pin is initially positioned on the axis such that its image coincides with it. If the concave section is subsequently filled with water ($\mu = 4/3$), determine the distance through which the pin must be moved to ensure the image once again coincides with the pin.
questions.solution:
For the glass lens, the top surface is concave and the bottom surface is convex. Since it rests on the convex surface, light from the pin enters the concave surface. Taking the downward direction as positive, the radius of the first surface is $R_1 = -60$ cm and the radius of the second surface is $R_2 = -20$ cm.

The power of the glass lens is given by:
$P_g = (\mu_g - 1) \left( \dfrac{1}{R_1} - \dfrac{1}{R_2} \right)$
$P_g = (1.5 - 1) \left( \dfrac{1}{-60} - \dfrac{1}{-20} \right) = 0.5 \left( \dfrac{1}{20} - \dfrac{1}{60} \right) = \dfrac{1}{60} \text{ cm}^{-1}$

The bottom surface is silvered and acts as a mirror for light traveling inside the glass. Its radius of curvature is $R_2 = -20$ cm.
Power of the equivalent mirror:
$P_m = -\dfrac{2}{R_2} = -\dfrac{2}{-20} = \dfrac{1}{10} \text{ cm}^{-1}$

The equivalent power of the initial system is:
$P = 2P_g + P_m = 2 \left( \dfrac{1}{60} \right) + \dfrac{1}{10} = \dfrac{1}{30} + \dfrac{1}{10} = \dfrac{4}{30} = \dfrac{2}{15} \text{ cm}^{-1}$

The equivalent focal length is $F = \dfrac{15}{2} = 7.5$ cm. For the image to coincide with the pin, the pin must be at the center of curvature of the equivalent mirror.
Initial position $u_1 = 2F = 15$ cm.

When water is filled in the concave section, a plano-convex water lens is formed with $R_{w1} = \infty$ and $R_{w2} = -60$ cm.
Power of the water lens:
$P_w = (\mu_w - 1) \left( \dfrac{1}{R_{w1}} - \dfrac{1}{R_{w2}} \right) = \left( \dfrac{4}{3} - 1 \right) \left( 0 - \dfrac{1}{-60} \right) = \dfrac{1}{180} \text{ cm}^{-1}$

The new equivalent power of the system is:
$P' = 2P_w + P = 2 \left( \dfrac{1}{180} \right) + \dfrac{2}{15} = \dfrac{1}{90} + \dfrac{12}{90} = \dfrac{13}{90} \text{ cm}^{-1}$

The new equivalent focal length is $F' = \dfrac{90}{13}$ cm.
New position for the image to coincide is $u_2 = 2F' = \dfrac{180}{13} \approx 13.85$ cm.

Distance the pin must be moved is:
$\Delta u = u_1 - u_2 = 15 - \dfrac{180}{13} = \dfrac{15}{13} \approx 1.15 \text{ cm}$

Since $u_2 < u_1$, the pin must be moved towards the lens. The closest matching option provided is $1.14 \text{ cm}$ towards the lens.
